segments.say: And none of this was ever about code. Twelve PDFs in a folder. Receipts - vendors, dates, line items, totals. Nothing in this folder is code and nothing in it has anything to do with this project. That is deliberate: this is the lecture that generalises furthest, and it is the one that will still be useful when everything else in the week is a version behind.

The sort of thing that arrives attached to an email and gets typed into a spreadsheet by somebody on a Tuesday. So: one document, one line of structured output, and the schema in the prompt rather than in a hope. Vendor. Date. Currency as a three-letter code, inferred from the symbol. Total as a number. Items as an integer count. No prose, no code fence. Being that specific is the entire difference between output you can parse and output you have to read. And read what came back for the first one. A vendor, a date, a currency, a total and a count. One line, no preamble, no explanation of what a receipt is, no offer to help further. Well - almost. The currency came back null, because the PDF has no symbol anywhere and its twenty percent VAT line fits three countries, and it added a line underneath saying so. It refused to guess. That is what asking for a schema buys you, and it is the difference between a demo and a step in a pipeline.

Then the same thing twelve times, from a shell loop. Not a batch feature, not a queue, not an integration - a for loop, appending one line of JSON per file. This is the beat that replaces a whole desktop application, and it is four lines of shell. The folder is twelve files, r01 to r12, and the loop takes them by glob in that order. Read is again the only tool it is allowed, so the entire effect of twelve sessions on this machine is twelve lines of text on standard output. Nothing writes, nothing runs, nothing asks. That is not a small detail when you are pointing an agent at a folder of documents you did not write and cannot fully vouch for. And count what is not in it: no worker pool, no retry, no state, no resume. If one of the twelve fails you get eleven lines and a gap, and you run that one again. For a folder of twelve that is exactly the right amount of machinery, and knowing when it is the right amount is worth more than knowing how to build the other kind. The prompt changed shape too, and it matters. The single-document version had the filename typed into it inside single quotes. This one is in double quotes so the shell expands the variable, which is the whole trick: one instruction, twelve substitutions. Get the quoting wrong and every session reads a file literally called dollar f, and you get twelve identical errors. There is one more thing in that loop worth pointing at, which is the redirection. Each answer appends to a file. Not a database, not a queue - a file, which you can open, and read, and diff, and delete a bad line out of. For a job this size the right storage is the one you can fix with a text editor at four in the afternoon.

And it is worth being clear about what this costs, because a loop hides it. Twelve documents is twelve separate sessions, each one starting from nothing, reading a PDF, and answering. There is no shared context and no discount for the eleventh one being similar to the first. That is fine at twelve. At twelve thousand it is a number you want to have looked at first, which is what the cost field in the last lecture was for. And there is a precondition hiding under all of this. These PDFs have text in them. The Read tool pulls that text out, which is why one line of instruction is enough - and if these had been photographs of receipts, scanned at an angle by somebody's phone, you would be asking a different question with a different failure rate. Test that first, on the worst document in the pile, before you write the loop. The technique is cheap. Finding out on document nine hundred that half your inputs are pictures is not. And be honest about the failure mode you are signing up for. Twelve sessions, twelve independent judgements, and no two of them can be compared against each other while they are running. If the fourth one misreads a column heading, nothing anywhere notices - not the loop, not the file, not the total at the bottom. The check has to be a separate pass, afterwards, and it has to be one you actually write.

The other thing a loop hides is order. These are independent, so nothing here needs them in sequence - and the only reason they are is that a for loop is four characters and a job queue is an afternoon. If this were twelve thousand you would want three or four running at once, and you already know how to write that, because we wrote it two lectures ago and it was thirty lines. Look at what the loop prints while it waits. A dash and a filename, r01 through r12 in order, and that echo is doing real work: without it this is three minutes of a blinking cursor and no way to tell a slow document from a hung one. There is a delete at the front of the line too. The output is appended, so running this twice without clearing the file gives you twenty-four lines and a silently wrong total. And the schema in this version has one key the single-document run did not: the filename. Twelve independent sessions produce twelve lines that look alike, and nothing else in the loop records which document each one came from. It is also worth watching the loop run rather than skipping it, because the rhythm is the point. Roughly twenty seconds a document, one after another, no acceleration and no coordination. That is what this technique looks like at any scale: the same twenty seconds, multiplied. And DONE at the bottom, so you know the shell reached the end rather than the last one dying quietly. Hold the wall-clock against the alternative: a person opening twelve PDFs and typing twelve rows into a spreadsheet, which is also not instant. That comparison is the only one that matters, and it is the one nobody makes before they go and build the queue instead. Which makes the arithmetic easy and makes the decision about whether to run it a decision you can actually make.

Twelve PDFs in, one table out, with a total on the bottom. The raw file first, because it is not clean. Half the lines have caveats attached - no currency symbol anywhere, a twenty percent VAT line that hints at Britain but is not a symbol. The prose I banned. And two things are wrong with it, both worth stopping on. Five of the twelve have a currency and seven are blank - same instruction, same model, same kind of document, and half of them decided it was not stated and returned nothing rather than guessing. That is arguably the right behaviour and it is certainly the honest one, and it makes the column unusable. If you need a field to be present you do not ask nicely for it; you check afterwards and re-run the ones that are missing. That is what the grep in front of jq is doing - keeping only the lines that start with a brace. And the total: two thousand eight hundred and fifty-six point eight nine, followed by eleven more digits. That is floating point doing what floating point does, in my jq, not in the model. It is exactly the sort of thing that ships - because the interesting part worked, and the moment the interesting part works your attention moves on and everything downstream of it stops being read.

Nothing in that loop knew it was reading receipts. Change the schema and it reads invoices, or survey responses, or six hundred markdown files. The agent is not the product here. The loop is. The only thing you would change for a different job is the list of keys in that sentence. Everything either side of it stays exactly as it is. Which is the sentence I would leave this day on. Everything this week has been about code because that is where the tooling grew up.
